study.title: No Conductor Needed
study.question: How do small groups rehearse on their own?
study.passage:
Small-ensemble rehearsal guide (written for this lesson):
Groups: duets, trios, quartets or quintets (e.g. brass quintet: 2 trumpets, horn, trombone, tuba; woodwind quintet: flute, oboe, clarinet, horn, bassoon; mixed groups and percussion ensembles also work).
Rehearsal plan (write before you start): 1. Tune together (2 minutes). 2. Warm up with a unison scale (3 minutes). 3. Run the piece once without stopping to find problems (4 minutes). 4. Fix two problem spots (15 minutes): name the bar, the problem and the fix. 5. Run again (4 minutes). 6. Set goals for next rehearsal (2 minutes).
Starting together: one player gives a silent count-off or breath cue with the instrument (one bar of tempo).
Independence: each player must count their own rests; use the score to see how parts fit. If you get lost, listen for the melody.
Respectful rehearsals: comments are about the music ("bar 12 rhythm doesn't line up"), not the person; everyone suggests fixes.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Form a small group and choose a piece
Run, fix two spots and run again
discussion: How did you start together without a conductor?
How did your group give feedback respectfully?
study.product: Lead a small-group rehearsal using a written plan, fixing two problem spots, and report the results.

body.hook: Watch a string quartet and you'll see tiny head nods, raised eyebrows and breaths that start and stop the music. Leading and following without words is a skill every ensemble musician needs.

study.title: Lead and Follow
study.question: How do small ensembles communicate without words?
study.passage:
Cueing guide (written for this lesson):
Start cue: the leader lifts the instrument slightly on the upbeat, breathes in tempo, and moves down on beat 1. Everyone breathes with the leader.
Release cue: a small circle or lift of the bell or head on the final note, ending with a clear stop.
Tempo change: the leader shows a slower or faster motion with the instrument; others watch.
Fermatas: the leader holds and shows the release.
Who leads? Usually the player with the melody or the most rhythmic part leads that section; the lead can pass ("handoff") during the piece. Mark "L" in your part where you lead.
Activities: 1. Silent starts: groups start and stop a single chord using only breath cues. 2. Tempo game: the leader varies tempo in a scale; followers match. 3. Handoffs: decide who leads each section of your piece and mark it. 4. Eyes up: memorize the first bar so you can look at the leader on the start.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Plan handoffs and mark "L" in parts

body.objective: Students will be able to perform a small-ensemble piece.

successCriteria: I can perform a small-ensemble piece with independence and communication

body.hook: Performance day for your small ensemble: no conductor, no full band to hide behind. Just you, your group and an audience. It's one of the most rewarding performances a musician can give.

study.title: Ensemble Showcase
study.question: How do we give a polished small-ensemble performance?
study.passage:
Showcase plan (written for this lesson):
Before: final rehearsal with a full run; check chairs and stands setup so everyone can see each other (semicircle).
Introduction (30 seconds): one member says the group's name, the piece title, the composer or arranger, and one thing to listen for.
Performance: leader cues the start; follow your planned handoffs; if something goes wrong, keep going and use cues to stay together.
After: group bow together on a cue.
Rubric (each 1–4): tone and intonation; rhythm and togetherness; dynamics and expression; communication (cues and eye contact); stage presence and introduction.
Assessment: watch a recording if possible; each member rates the group and writes one strength and one goal. Audience members give two "glows" and one "grow" to other groups.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Set up in a semicircle for sightlines
discussion: How did your introduction set up the performance?
Were your cues clear on stage?
How did you recover from any mistakes?
What was your group's biggest strength?
study.product: Perform your small-ensemble piece with an introduction, and complete a group assessment using the rubric.
